analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **RCT, R 1:1, n=60**, iADT alone vs iADT + SBRT. Phase, blinding, site count and median follow-up are not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biochemically recurrent prostate cancer (or de novo metastatic), hormone-sensitive. **PSA >0.1 ng/mL** after prior RadP or **≥2** after prior radical RT, **negative conventional staging (CT, bone scan)**, and **≤3 metastatic deposits on PSMA PET (miN1, miM1)**.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: **8-9 months ADT, then stop**. ADT agent not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SBRT per **institutional protocols** based on the anatomic region irradiated, delivered as early as possible and **within 4 months of ADT**. Dose, fractionation and target volume are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Feasibility met with **91%** of eligible pts enrolled. Arm-level efficacy is in the table; QoL values are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: STOMP and ORIOLE tested MDT against observation without hormone therapy. EXTEND added MDT to intermittent hormone therapy, the closest design. STOP moves that question to **PSMA PET-positive, conventional-imaging-negative** disease.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCR or de novo metastatic HSPC with negative conventional staging and ≤3 PSMA PET deposits (miN1, miM1). Does not represent conventional-imaging-visible metastatic disease or more than 3 PSMA PET deposits.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Biochemical progression definition and testosterone recovery after ADT cessation are not in source, and both shape a PSA endpoint. SBRT dose varied by institution. The source tweet is truncated, so the 3-yr ADT re-initiation rates are missing.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: With the ADT course held constant, the biochemical gap is an **SBRT-attributable** signal. It does not settle whether that converts into longer time off ADT (**p=0.06**), MFS or OS, or whether SBRT alone would do as well.

studies.interpretation:
The design question here is narrower and cleaner than in most metastasis-directed therapy trials. Both arms received the same finite course of ADT and then stopped, so the comparison isolates what SBRT adds once the systemic backbone is held constant. STOMP and ORIOLE compared MDT against observation, with no hormone therapy in either arm. EXTEND tested MDT added to intermittent hormone therapy in oligometastatic prostate cancer, which is the closest precedent in logic. STOP moves that same question into disease that only PSMA PET can see, with CT and bone scan negative, which is the population now filling clinics as PSMA PET replaces conventional staging at recurrence.

The efficacy readout is biochemical progression: 21% vs 60% at 3 years, p=0.004, with the median not reached vs 27 mo. Biochemical progression after stopping ADT is a soft endpoint. It depends on how fast testosterone recovers, how often PSA is drawn and how progression is defined, and the source gives none of these. The control arm figure is still informative on its own terms: a majority of men given 8-9 months of ADT alone had progressed biochemically by 3 years, which argues that a finite hormone course without local consolidation does not hold PSMA PET-only disease for long.

Several features should temper confidence in the size of the effect. The trial enrolled 60 men and its stated success was feasibility, with 91% of eligible pts enrolled, so the efficacy comparison carries wide uncertainty and no confidence interval appears in the source. A p-value of this size in a trial this small can rest on a handful of events. The endpoint closest to what a patient feels, re-initiation of ADT, came in at p=0.06 and did not reach the conventional threshold. Re-initiation is a clinician decision, and blinding is not stated, so that endpoint is open to knowledge of arm in either direction. A QoL slide was shown but no values were captured, and toxicity is absent from the source entirely.

For a radiation oncologist the transferability gap is technique. SBRT followed institutional protocols by anatomic region, with no dose, fractionation or target volume in the source. Nodal (miN1) and distant (miM1) deposits are pooled, so the trial says nothing about whether pelvic nodal recurrences are better served by SBRT to the involved node or by elective nodal RT, and no in-field vs out-of-field failure data are given. The timing parameter is the one concrete instruction: SBRT as early as possible and within 4 months of ADT.

What this supports is the already common habit of consolidating PSMA PET-only oligometastatic HSPC with SBRT when a short ADT course is being given. What it leaves untouched is whether ADT is needed at all alongside SBRT, and whether intensified hormonal therapy would erase the difference. The result would be misleading if the PSA separation reflects delayed biochemical relapse without a matching delay in metastatic progression or castration resistance, and only a larger trial with MFS and time-off-ADT endpoints can answer that.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: ADT was fixed at 8-9 months in both arms, so the 21% vs 60% 3-yr biochemical progression gap isolates SBRT, delivered within 4 months of ADT. Dose, fractionation and target volume followed institutional protocols and are not in source. miN1 and miM1 are pooled, so SBRT vs elective nodal RT stays open.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: A finite 8-9 month ADT course alone left 60% with biochemical progression at 3 yr, vs 21% with SBRT added. The time-off-ADT read is weaker: re-initiation of ADT p=0.06. No ARPI intensification arm, so the hormonal backbone question is untouched.

studies.name: PACE-A
studies.tldr: SBRT 36.25 Gy/5fx vs prostatectomy: 13 BCF events, HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.16-1.46), p=0.18; 5-yr BCF-free 94.8% vs 94.1% in localised low/intermediate-risk PCa.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III, open-label, multicohort RCT** (PACE); PACE-A randomised **1:1** to SBRT or prostatectomy. **N=123** (63 SBRT, 60 prostatectomy) from 8 centres per the abstract, August 2012 to February 2022. **Median follow-up 8 years** (IQR 6.1-8.0); analysis by intention to treat.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men with **localised prostate cancer, cT1-T2, Gleason ≤3+4, PSA ≤20 ng/mL**, MRI staged, who were **suitable candidates for prostatectomy**. Median age 65.5 years (IQR 60.5-68.6), median PSA 7.9 ng/mL (IQR 5.9-11.0); **5.7% low-risk and 94.3% intermediate-risk**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions over 1-2 weeks**, with **no ADT permitted**. Target volume, margins, platform and any intraprostatic boost are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Comparator was radical prostatectomy by open, laparoscopic or robot-assisted approach. The split between approaches and nodal dissection practice is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Freedom from biochemical/clinical failure**: PSA rise (**nadir+2 ng/ml post-RT or >0.2 ng/ml post-prostatectomy**), ADT start, recurrence, metastases or prostate cancer death. The source does not state whether this was the prespecified primary endpoint or give a non-inferiority margin. Function by EPIC-26 and clinician-reported CTCAE.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **13 BCF events** (5 SBRT, 8 prostatectomy), **unadjusted HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.16-1.46; p=0.18)**. BCF-free at 5 years **94.8% (84.6, 98.3) SBRT vs 94.1% (82.6, 98.1) prostatectomy**; at 8 years 91.2% (80.1, 96.2) vs 83.7% (68.4, 92.0). Seven deaths, none from prostate cancer.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: At 5 years, **≥1 urinary pad in 3/36 (8.3%) SBRT vs 14/29 (48%) prostatectomy**. Moderate/big bowel problem in 0 SBRT vs 1/28 (3.6%) prostatectomy. Clinician-reported **G≥2 GI 1/54 (2%) vs 0** and **G≥2 GU 2/53 (3.8%) vs 1/40 (2.5%)**, SBRT vs prostatectomy. Sexual function is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ProtecT is the randomised reference for surgery against radiotherapy in localised disease, using conventionally fractionated RT rather than SBRT. PACE-B, a sibling cohort of the same trial, compared SBRT with longer-course RT in men not headed for surgery. This is the direct randomised SBRT against prostatectomy efficacy comparison that the abstract describes as lacking.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with low or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer (cT1-T2, Gleason ≤3+4, PSA ≤20 ng/mL) who are surgical candidates and treated without ADT. Does not represent disease above Gleason 3+4 or PSA 20 ng/mL, or men receiving ADT with RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Failure thresholds differ by arm**, so PSA failure is detectable earlier after surgery than after SBRT. The 5-year pad figures rest on **36 and 29 respondents** of 63 and 60 randomised. The tweet reports 10 centres against the abstract's 8, and the slide labels the absolute-difference interval 90% CI where the abstract says 95%.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The 5-year rates are near identical and the 8-year gap rests on few men at risk, so the defensible read is **no detectable difference**, not SBRT superiority. The continence contrast is the largest effect in the dataset and the bowel penalty usually set against RT is **not visible** here. It does not settle metastasis or mortality outcomes.

studies.interpretation:
Men choosing between surgery and radiotherapy for localised prostate cancer have long been counselled on the assumption that cancer control is equivalent and that function is the tiebreaker. ProtecT gave that assumption randomised support for conventionally delivered radiotherapy, and PACE-B placed SBRT alongside longer-course RT. What had not been done was to randomise SBRT directly against prostatectomy for efficacy, and the abstract is explicit that such evidence was lacking. That is the gap this dataset fills, and it is also why the size of the trial matters so much to how it should be read.

The efficacy result is 13 events among 123 men. A hazard ratio of 0.48 with an interval running from 0.16 to 1.46 is compatible with SBRT being considerably better and with it being meaningfully worse. No non-inferiority margin appears in the source, so "comparable" is the investigators' description of overlapping estimates, not a tested claim. The 5-year figures, 94.8% and 94.1%, are the honest summary. The 8-year figures of 91.2% and 83.7% look like late divergence in favour of SBRT, but they sit on a shrinking number at risk and should not be read as a durable advantage.

The endpoint definition deserves more weight than the headline gives it. Failure after SBRT required a rise to nadir+2 ng/ml, while failure after prostatectomy was triggered at >0.2 ng/ml. Those thresholds are not equally sensitive. A surgical recurrence is declared early and at low disease burden; a post-radiotherapy recurrence is declared later by construction. Any comparison of biochemical failure across these two modalities therefore leans toward radiotherapy, and a trial with this few events cannot absorb that lean. The salvage data are a partial check: radiotherapy in 5 prostatectomy pts, surgery in 1 SBRT pt, with ADT in 3 and 2. These point the same way, but they are not symmetric either, since salvage RT after surgery is a routine, low-threshold step and salvage after SBRT is not. With 7 deaths and none from prostate cancer, the hard endpoints are silent.

The functional data carry the clearest signal. Pad use at 5 years in 3/36 (8.3%) after SBRT against 14/29 (48%) after prostatectomy is a large contrast, and the bowel penalty normally set against radiotherapy does not appear: no SBRT pt reported a moderate or big bowel problem, and clinician-graded G≥2 GI toxicity was 1/54. The caution is the denominators. Responses came from 36 and 29 men of 63 and 60 randomised, and nothing in the source says whether non-responders differed. Sexual function, the third leg of this counselling conversation, is not in the source.

Generalisability is narrow in a specific way. Recruiting 123 men between August 2012 and February 2022 shows how few accept randomisation between an operation and radiotherapy, so those who did are a selected group. The cohort was 94.3% intermediate risk, capped at Gleason 3+4, and treated without ADT. The result informs the counselling of a surgical candidate in that band who is weighing SBRT. It leaves untouched higher-grade disease, RT combined with ADT, and nodal treatment. It would be overturned by longer follow-up showing divergence in metastasis or in salvage burden once more events accrue.

At 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions without ADT, this informs counselling surgical candidates on definitive SBRT.

Approach (open, laparoscopic, robot assisted) was mixed and its split is not reported in source.

verdict.audience: Newly diagnosed brain met, index lesion 2.0-7.0 cm, indicated for resection

studies.significance: The control was not a weak arm: 92.2% got multi-fraction cavity SRT (27 Gy/3 or 30 Gy/5) and 12-mo SBR was 15.4%, in line with published fractionated series. The SBR HR stayed 0.06 in per-protocol while OS did not hold (HR 0.73, p=0.2156), so the cavity-control decision moves, the survival claim does not. TBRT prescription dose is not in the source text.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a newly diagnosed brain metastasis 2.0-7.0 cm indicated for resection, this supports intraoperative Cs-131 tile placement as an alternative to post-op cavity SRT for surgical bed control; it does not address unresected lesions, which received SRT in both arms.

primary_endpoint.name: Time to surgical bed recurrence (co-primary with SB-RFS)

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized, open-label, non-inferiority phase 3** across 32 US centers; 240 consented, **230 randomized 1:1 pre-operatively** (115 per arm). Efficacy in the pre-specified mITT population (**103 R+TBRT, 101 R+SRT**). Median follow-up **12.9 mo** (IQR 5.9-22.8); data cut-off October 2025.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Newly diagnosed brain metastases indicated for resection, with **one surgical index metastasis 2.0-7.0 cm**. mITT required surgery, pathologically confirmed metastasis, and any follow-up information; 14 did not have surgery, 11 had ineligible pathology, 1 had no follow-up.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **R+TBRT:** collagen tiles each carrying four Cs-131 seeds implanted in the cavity at resection, with post-op CT for dosimetry; prescription dose not reported in source text. **R+SRT:** volume-dependent cavity SRT, **17-20 Gy/1, 27 Gy/3 or 30 Gy/5**, planned 21±7 days from surgery, multi-fraction in **92.2%**, median start 27.0 days (range 6-47). Non-index metastases received SRT in both arms.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary:** time-to-SBR (death censored) and SB-RFS (SBR or death), with site-reported SBR centrally reviewed by two neuroradiologists. **Secondary:** OS, FACT-Br QoL, KPS, Barthel ADL, neurocognition, LMD, RN (site-reported). NI margin **HR 1.26**; fixed hierarchy from non-inferiority to superiority to OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Non-inferiority and then superiority** were met for both co-primaries. Local control findings held across mITT, ITT and per-protocol populations; the OS difference did not hold in per-protocol.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Any AE in **83 pts (79.0%)** with R+TBRT vs **67 (80.7%)** with R+SRT, risk difference -1.7% (95% CI -13.2 to 9.8). ≥G3 TRAEs **20.0% vs 21.7%**. 12-mo RN **5.3% vs 5.7%** (HR 0.85, p=0.76). No differences in FACT-Br, KPS, Barthel ADL or neurocognition.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Post-op cavity SRT became standard on trials showing better surgical bed control than observation; Mahajan et al. reported 12-month freedom-from-SBR of **72%** with single-fraction SRT vs 43% with observation. Multi-institutional fractionated series report **84-87%**, and the ROADS control arm (12-mo SBR 15.4%) sits in that range, so tiles beat a contemporary comparator.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with a newly diagnosed brain metastasis 2.0-7.0 cm indicated for resection at US centers able to implant Cs-131 tiles. Does not represent unresected metastases, which received SRT in both arms, or pts found intra-operatively to have non-metastatic pathology.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Central reviewers were not told the assignment, but **seed susceptibility artifact** on MRI may have revealed it, and RN was site-reported. The SB-RFS definition was corrected in May 2025 (death had been specified as a censoring event), creating two co-primaries. No granular systemic therapy data, so the OS mechanism cannot be examined.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The surgical bed control result is consistent across analysis populations and rests on few events (1 vs 12). The OS difference is unexplained by distant brain failure or LMD, did not persist in per-protocol, and the authors state it **requires validation**. How tiles compare with pre-operative SRT (NCT03741673, NCT05438212) is untested.

studies.interpretation:
The comparator is the first thing to check when an experimental arm wins by this margin, and here it holds up. The R+SRT arm was contemporary practice: multi-fraction cavity SRT in 92.2%, with a 12-month cumulative incidence of surgical bed recurrence of 15.4%. The authors set that against the 84-87% 12-month freedom-from-SBR reported in multi-institutional fractionated series, and it is ahead of the 72% Mahajan et al. reported with single-fraction cavity SRT. The HR of 0.06 is therefore not manufactured by an underperforming control.

What should temper the read is how few events carry it. One SBR in the tile arm against 12 with SRT gives a CI of 0.01-0.46, at a median follow-up of 12.9 months. The direction is not in doubt, the size is imprecise, and later or marginal failures after a brachytherapy source with a different dose delivery profile cannot be excluded at this follow-up. The SB-RFS co-primary is a different kind of evidence: with 30 vs 45 events against 1 vs 12 recurrences, most of what it counts is death, so it largely restates the survival difference instead of adding independent support for local control.

The OS result deserves the most skepticism. A median of 42.5 vs 17.6 months from swapping one focal cavity technique for another, with no difference in distant brain failure (HR 0.93) and none in LMD, is hard to attribute to local control alone. The mITT control arm includes 18 pts who never received SRT, 8 of whom died and 3 of whom entered hospice before it could be delivered. Those pts mark early systemic decline as much as a treatment failure. Restricted to pts who received assigned treatment, the OS HR moves to 0.73 with p=0.2156, while the SBR HR stays at 0.06. The authors argue the per-protocol cut introduces immortal time bias, which is fair, but the truth plausibly lies between the two analyses, and they themselves say the OS finding requires validation. The upper bound of the tile-arm median was not estimable.

Two design points cut in opposite directions. The SB-RFS definition was amended in May 2025 after the protocol was found to censor death, which is why there are two co-primaries; the authors state no outcome data had been reviewed by then, and time-to-SBR is the endpoint a radiation oncologist would have wanted anyway. Central review was by neuroradiologists not told the assignment, but seed artifact makes the tile arm identifiable on MRI, so blinding was nominal. RN was site-reported at 5.3% vs 5.7% at 12 months, and separating necrosis from recurrence in a seeded cavity is exactly where knowledge of the arm matters. The composite SBR-or-RN HR of 0.28 offers some protection against that misclassification.

The decision this moves is narrow: for a metastasis already going to resection, whether the cavity is treated in the operating room or at a median of 27.0 days afterward. A 17.8% non-completion rate for post-operative SRT, in line with the 20% Brennan et al. reported and the 73% completion Yeboa et al. reported, means part of the tile advantage is simply that every pt gets treated, a property of the pathway that should transfer to practice. It leaves unresected lesions untouched, and it does not say how tiles compare with pre-operative SRT, under test in two randomized phase 3 trials (NCT03741673, NCT05438212). The tile prescription dose is not in the source text, which limits any attempt to separate a dose effect from a timing effect.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The control was not a weak arm: 92.2% got multi-fraction cavity SRT (27 Gy/3 or 30 Gy/5) and 12-mo SBR was 15.4%, in line with published fractionated series. The SBR HR stayed 0.06 in per-protocol while OS did not hold (HR 0.73, p=0.2156). TBRT prescription dose is not in the source text.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Randomization was pre-operative, but tiles went in only after intra-operative pathologic confirmation: 11 randomized pts had ineligible pathology, including GBM cases that received no TBRT. Adjuvant radiation is completed at resection, against 17.8% of the SRT arm never receiving it. Median craniotomy stay was 3.0 vs 4.0 days (p=0.56).

studies.monday_clinic: In LS or ES-SCLC with a clean brain MRI after first-line therapy and access to q3-month MRI in year 1, this supports surveillance alone over PCI, including HA-PCI; it does not extend to pts who cannot complete MRI surveillance.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International **randomized phase III**, **304 pts** randomly assigned 01/2020 to 12/2025. Stratified by stage (LS/ES), receipt of IO, and PS (0-1 vs 2). Median follow-up for living pts **22 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **LS or ES-SCLC** after completing initial therapy, with **no BM on MRI** before enrollment. **68% LS-SCLC**, 41% received immunotherapy with upfront treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **PCI 25 Gy in 10 fx**, hippocampal avoidance at physician discretion (**77% HA-PCI**). At brain metastases, RT was recommended in both arms, WBRT or SRS allowed.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** CFFS, time to first cognitive failure on any of HVLT-R, COWA, or Trail Making, or death, by 1-sided 0.05 log-rank. **Key secondary:** OS non-inferiority with MRI alone, margin 1.25 on the upper 90% CI. MRI and cognitive testing q3 months in year 1, q6 months in year 2.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: CFFS favored MRI alone across stage and HA-PCI analyses (table above). **Interim OS HR 0.90** (90% CI 0.67-1.20) at 128 deaths, and cognitive failure by Fine-Gray gave a subdistribution HR of 0.62. BM were decreased with PCI with **no PFS difference**, magnitudes not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: The toxicity signal is neurocognitive: objective failure was more frequent with PCI. Day 180 patient-reported cognitive concerns were **not different** (PROMIS p=0.07, MDASI p=0.69), while longitudinal modeling favored MRI alone. Other toxicities not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source frames the PCI benefit (fewer BM, better OS) as coming from **pre-MRI era** studies. Takahashi's Japanese randomized trial had already questioned PCI under MRI surveillance in ES-SCLC, and NRG CC003 tested hippocampal avoidance within PCI. This is the first randomized readout covering LS-SCLC under MRI surveillance.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents LS or ES-SCLC with no brain metastases on MRI after initial therapy, followed with scheduled MRI through 24 months. Does not represent pts without restaging brain MRI or without access to q3-month MRI surveillance.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The CFFS table lists **115 and 107 pts** against 151 and 152 randomized, with no explanation in source. Slide and abstract p-values differ. The prespecified Day 180 PRO endpoints were negative, so the patient-reported benefit rests on longitudinal modeling.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Hippocampal avoidance did not rescue PCI on this endpoint, which leaves OS as the only argument for prophylaxis. The interim OS estimate is compatible with non-inferiority but is not the final analysis, and **22 months** is short for LS pts with curative intent.

studies.interpretation:
The case for PCI in SCLC was built before MRI could reliably show that the brain was clean at restaging or catch small relapses while they were still treatable. The abstract says as much: the reductions in brain metastases and the survival benefit come from pre-MRI era studies. In extensive stage, Takahashi's Japanese randomized trial had already undercut that case once MRI surveillance was the comparator, and many clinicians stopped offering PCI there. Limited stage is where the habit persisted, because the older pooled evidence was never retested. MAVERICK matters mostly because of who it enrolled: 68% LS-SCLC, with a stage interaction that is nowhere near positive on either the slide (p=0.79) or the abstract (p=0.92).

The primary endpoint deserves a careful read before the HR is taken at face value. CFFS counts a decline on any one of three tests, or death, as an event, so it is built to be sensitive. Both arms fail fast: 6 month CFFS is 37.8% with MRI alone and 16.5% with PCI, and by 12 months the figures are 17.3% and 5.9%. That is not a picture of preserved cognition without PCI. It is a population in which chemotherapy, disease and death drive most events, with PCI bringing them forward. The Fine-Gray analysis (subdistribution HR 0.62) argues that the difference sits in cognitive failure itself and is not carried by deaths. The 1-sided 0.05 test and 90% intervals are more permissive than the usual convention, though an upper bound of 0.78 leaves some distance from the null.

The most useful secondary result for a radiation oncologist is the hippocampal avoidance analysis. With 77% of PCI delivered as HA-PCI, and pts in the MRI arm who had been declared for HA-PCI before randomization still doing better (HR 0.63), the obvious rejoinder, that modern PCI is cognitively safe, loses its footing on this endpoint. NRG CC003 asked whether hippocampal avoidance improves on conventional PCI. MAVERICK asks the harder question of whether either beats not irradiating at all.

What the trial has not yet delivered is the survival answer that the standard-of-care claim depends on. The key secondary is non-inferiority with a margin of 1.25 on the upper 90% bound, and the interim estimate of 0.90 (0.67-1.20) comes at 128 of a planned 190 deaths. The direction is reassuring, but an interim read is not the final one. Brain metastases were less frequent with PCI and PFS was no different, which fits a model where MRI-detected relapses are salvaged with SRS or WBRT without a survival cost. That model depends on scan adherence the trial enforced and routine practice may not. The result would be wrong if late OS diverges in LS pts, where median follow-up of 22 months is short and an isolated brain relapse can cost a cure.

Two reporting details temper confidence at the margins. The slide and abstract give different p-values, which suggests different data cuts, and the CFFS table lists fewer pts than were randomized without explanation. The prespecified Day 180 patient-reported endpoints were also negative (p=0.07 and 0.69), so the objective tests show harm more clearly than pts report it. Finally, ADRIATIC changed LS-SCLC care during accrual, and only 41% received upfront immunotherapy. The IO interaction (p=0.25) is not a signal, but the durvalumab-consolidated LS pt is only partly represented here.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The HA-PCI escape route is closed: 77% of PCI was hippocampal-avoidant, and MRI-arm pts pre-declared for HA-PCI still did better (HR 0.63, 90% CI 0.47-0.83). Omission of PCI at 25 Gy/10 fx now hinges on OS, where the interim upper bound of 1.20 sits inside the 1.25 margin.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The CFFS benefit of skipping PCI did not differ by receipt of upfront IO (interaction p=0.25), but only 41% received it and ADRIATIC landed mid-accrual. For referral decisions after first-line therapy, the commitment shifts to scheduled brain MRI q3 months in year 1, q6 months in year 2.

papers.title: Efficacy of Radical Prostatectomy Versus Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT) for Localised Prostate Cancer: Results from an international Phase III Randomised Controlled Trial (PACE - A)
papers.abstract:
ASTRO 2026 abstract LBA 32 · PL 01 - Plenary Session · 2026-09-28 · presented by Nicholas van As, MD, MB

Purpose/Objective(s): Treatment selection for localised prostate cancer (LPCa) is often influenced by expected functional outcomes, assuming comparable cancer control between treatments. Randomised evidence comparing efficacy of radical prostatectomy and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is lacking.
Materials/Methods: PACE (NCT01584258) is phase III, open label, multicohort randomised controlled trial. In PACE-A, men with LPCa (cT1-T2, Gleason score =3+4, PSA =20 ng/mL) who were suitable candidates for prostatectomy were randomised (1:1) to SBRT or prostatectomy. SBRT was delivered to 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions over 1-2 weeks. Prostatectomy could be open, laparoscopic, or robot assisted. Androgen deprivation therapy was not permitted. Freedom from biochemical/clinical failure (BCF), based on PSA rises (nadir+2ng/ml or >0.2 ng/ml post radiotherapy or prostatectomy) or commencement of ADT or recurrence or metastases or prostate cancer death was analysed using Cox proportional hazards and log-rank test by intention to treat.
Results: 123 patients were randomised from 8 centres between August 2012 and February 2022 (60 prostatectomy, 63 SBRT). Baseline characteristics were well-balanced between groups. Median age was 65.5 years (IQR 60.5-68.6), median pre-treatment PSA was 7.9ng/mL (IQR 5.9-11.0), 5.7% and 94.3% of patients had low/intermediate-risk disease, respectively. With median follow-up of 8 years (IQR: 6.1 – 8.0), 13 BCF events had occurred (5 SBRT, 8 prostatectomy), unadjusted hazard ratio 0.48 (95% CI 0:16-1.46; p=0.18). The estimated absolute difference at 5 years (based on the HR) is 3.1% (95% CI -2.6, 5.0) with 5-year BCF-free rates 94.8% (84.6, 98.3) and 94.1% (82.6, 98.1) for SBRT and prostatectomy. 8-year rates were 91.2% (80.1, 96.2) and 83.7% (68.4, 92.0). Subsequent treatment for progression included surgery in 1 SBRT patient and radiotherapy in 5 prostatectomy patients. ADT was administered to 5 patients (3 prostatectomy, 2 SBRT). At 5 years, using Expanded Prostate Cancer Index Composite 26-item (EPIC-26) questionnaire, use of =1 urinary pad was reported by 3/36(8.3%) SBRT patients and 14/29(48%) prostatectomy patients. 1/28(3.6%) prostatectomy patient and 0 SBRT patients reported moderate/big bowel function problem. Clinician reported CTCAE grade =2 gastrointestinal side effects were reported by 1/54(2%) patient receiving SBRT and 0 prostatectomy patients. Grade =2 genitourinary side effects occurred in 2/53 (3.8%) receiving SBRT and1/40 (2.5%) patients undergoing prostatectomy.
Conclusion: With long-term follow-up, both prostatectomy and SBRT achieved excellent biochemical control in patients with localised prostate cancer. These findings support SBRT as an effective non-surgical treatment option with comparable long-term disease control to prostatectomy.

papers.title: SWOG S1827/MAVERICK: A Randomized Phase III Trial of Brain MRI Surveillance with and without Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI) for Small-Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)
papers.abstract:
ASTRO 2026 abstract LBA 03 · CT 01 - Clinical Trials Session · 2026-09-27 · presented by Paul Brown, MD

Purpose/Objective(s): For SCLC, studies from the pre-MRI era demonstrated a reduction in brain metastases (BM) and improved overall survival (OS) with PCI. We hypothesized that brain MRI surveillance without PCI would result in improved cognitive failure free survival (CFFS) without a decline in OS.
Materials/Methods: This international phase III trial enrolled patients (pts) with limited (LS) and extensive-stage (ES) SCLC who had completed initial therapy, with no BM on MRI prior to enrollment. Pts were randomized to MRI surveillance +/- PCI (25 Gy in 10 Fx), stratified by stage (LS/ES), receipt of immunotherapy (IO), and PS (0-1 vs 2). MRIs were q3 months during year 1 and q6 months during year 2 in both arms. Cognitive testing was performed at the same time points using the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised, Controlled Oral Word Association, and Trail Making Test. The primary objective was to compare CFFS defined as the time to first cognitive failure (CF) on any test or death, using a 1-sided 0.05 level log-rank test. The key secondary objective was to evaluate if OS was not inferior with MRI alone, with a non-inferiority margin for the upper bound 90% CI of 1.25. The final OS analysis will take place after 190 deaths. Additional objectives included comparing cumulative incidence of CF by Fine-Gray, BM-free survival, and toxicities. Patient reported cognitive concerns (via the MDASI-BT cognitive factor score and the PROMIS CFSF4a) and overall quality of life (QOL) (single-item LASA) were analyzed and preliminary results are presented.
Results: From 01/2020 to 12/2025, 304 pts were randomly assigned; 68% had LS-SCLC. The median follow-up for living pts is 22 months. CFFS was improved with MRI alone (HR 0.60, 90% CI 0.46-0.78, p=0.001). Subgroup analyses of CFFS demonstrated no significant differences in the benefit of MRI alone by either stage (LS/ES, interaction-p=0.92) or receipt of IO (yes/no, interaction-p=0.25). Of pts receiving PCI, 77% had hippocampal-avoidant (HA)-PCI. CFFS was superior for pts in the MRI arm who would have received HA-PCI (declared pre-randomization) compared to HA-PCI (HR 0.63, 90% CI 0.47-0.83, p=0.006). Preliminary analysis of OS at 128 deaths suggests no difference in OS (HR for MRI alone vs MRI+PCI: 0.90, 90% CI 0.67-1.20). There was a decreased risk of CF with MRI alone (subdistribution HR 0.62, 90% CI 0.48-0.79, p=0.001). At the Day 180 primary endpoint assessment for patient reported outcomes, no statistically significant differences in PROMIS or MDASI cognitive concerns (p=0.07 and 0.69, respectively) were found; however, pre-specified longitudinal modeling demonstrated improvements with MRI alone in PROMIS cognitive concerns that were significant at all time points and improved overall QOL on LASA at 90 and 180 days (all p<0.05).
Conclusion: Compared to MRI+PCI, MRI alone is associated with superior CFFS, reduced cognitive failure, and improvements in longitudinal QOL outcomes. These results support MRI surveillance alone as the standard of care for pts with SCLC.

papers.title: Surgery and tile-based radiation therapy versus surgery and stereotactic radiation for newly diagnosed brain metastases (ROADS): a randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial
papers.abstract: PURPOSE Post-operative stereotactic radiation (SRT) is the standard-of-care for resected brain metastases. Implantation of cesium-131 collagen tiles (tile-based radiation therapy, TBRT) initiates focal radiation immediately after resection, potentially offering therapeutic and logistical advantages. ROADS: a randomized, open-label, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial ( NCT04365374 ) compared the safety and efficacy of resection with TBRT (R+TBRT) to resection with SRT (R+SRT) for patients with a newly diagnosed brain metastasis indicated for surgical resection. PATIENTS AND METHODS Across 32 United States centers, patients were pre-operatively randomized 1:1 to resection R+TBRT or R+SRT. Any non-resected brain metastases received SRT post-operatively. Co-primary outcomes were time-to-surgical bed recurrence (SBR) and surgical bed recurrence-free survival (SB-RFS). Outcomes were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models with stratification factors as covariates. Multiplicity was controlled by hierarchical testing. Analyses used the pre-specified modified intent-to-treat (mITT) population (patients who underwent surgery, had pathologic confirmation of brain metastasis, and had follow-up information). RESULTS From April 2021 through August 2025, 230 patients were randomized (115 per arm); 204 of whom (103 R+TBRT, 101 R+SRT) comprised the mITT population. Median follow-up was 12.9 months. Median time-to-SBR was not reached (R+TBRT) versus 17.4 months (R+SRT) (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.06; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.01–0.46; p=0.0070). SB-RFS was improved with R+TBRT, with a median of not reached versus 10.9 months (R+SRT) (HR: 0.48; 95% CI: 0.30–0.76; p=0.0021). Overall adverse events did not appear to differ: 83 patients (79.0%, 95% CI: 70.0–86.4) (R+TBRT) versus 67 patients (80.7%, 95% CI:70.6–88.6) (R+SRT). CONCLUSION For patients with newly diagnosed brain metastases requiring resection, R+TBRT significantly improved SBR and SB-RFS, demonstrating both non-inferiority and superiority.
